text: The pressure that emptied the rest of the land came partly from a war the Potawatomi did not fight.
After lead was found around Galena in the 1820s, miners poured onto land the Sauk and Meskwaki still farmed, and pushed them west of the Mississippi.

In the spring of 1832, a sixty-five-year-old Sauk leader named Black Hawk led about a thousand Sauk, Meskwaki, and Kickapoo people, most of them women and children, back across the river to plant corn on land a disputed 1804 treaty had signed away.
Black Hawk and others said that treaty was never valid, that the men who signed it had no authority to sell.
Illinois settlers raised a militia anyway.
The Black Hawk War lasted from April to August.
It ended on the second of August at the mouth of the Bad Axe River in Wisconsin, where soldiers and militia fired on people trying to surrender under a white flag.
Of the thousand who had crossed in spring, roughly a hundred and fifty survived.
Its lesson for the government was simple.
Native nations that stayed could be removed, and the Northwest could be opened to settlers.
The Indian Removal Act of 1830 had already made that the policy of the country.
